tables.title: Table 1: Population Size Estimates among Men at Risk Using 3-Source Capture Recapture by survey site in Uganda, 2021 - 2023
context: Executive Summary

This report provides findings from a cross-sectional respondent-driven sampling (RDS) survey, which was conducted among Men at Risk. RDS is a probability-based chain-referral sampling method in which participants invite peers into the survey using coupons. This method was used to sample populations that lack a sampling frame. The BBS also incorporated the Capture Recapture method as population size estimation (PSE) methods to estimate the number of Men at Risk in each location.

The BBS were implemented from 2021 - 2023 by the Crane Survey Project, a collaborative activity of Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH), Ministry of Health (MoH), the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with funding from the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The BBS included 8 sites: Arua, Fort Portal, Gulu, Jinja, Kampala, Lira, Mbarara and Masaka.

The aim of the BBS was to inform HIV programming and policy in Uganda by estimating prevalence of HIV and syphilis, HIV service uptake (ART coverage, viral load suppression, and CD4 cell count) and HIV prevention services such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), risky behaviors (alcohol use, drug use) and depression. The eligibility criteria for survey participation were: males aged 18 years and over and who had had anal sex with another male in the 6 months that preceded the survey. Main survey findings are summarized in Tables 1-3 below.

context: Initial survey participants (“seeds”) were recruited by the survey team to start enrollment. Seeds were purposively enrolled to reflect a broad array of sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sexual orientation, education, area of residence, marital status, language, religion), HIV status, and affiliation with a KP organization or KP service provider. At the time of their enrollment, seeds were oriented to promote a feeling of survey ownership and enthusiasm about the project. Seeds were provided with coupons to distribute to their peers for enrollment. Instructions for peer recruitment using an enrollment process script were provided to seeds and participants. At the beginning of the survey about 2 – 5 seeds were included per site. The details regarding the number of seeds per site are included in section 2.4 on Seeds and Enrollment.

context: 2.2 Laboratory Testing

Laboratory testing was carried out both on-site and off-site. Nearby accredited/certified regional referral hospital laboratories conducted tests for CD4 count and provided viral load samples and DBS temporary storage. Central Public Health Laboratories (CPHL) was responsible for viral load testing and longer DBS storage. Testing using DBS was done at international laboratories at CDC in Atlanta, USA. Material Transfer Agreements (MTA) were signed to enable sample shipment outside Uganda.
2.2.1 Laboratory Procedures

Participants who were eligible and consented had venous blood drawn of up to 10 ml of blood in EDTA-containing vacutainer tubes. Blood was stored at room temperature or kept at 2-8°C at nearby peripheral hub and later transported to the CPHL where specimens were tested for HIV and CD4+ T cell counts. Specimen (plasma) were also prepared and transported to CPHL for storage at -20°C and -80 °C with consent of participants to allow future testing. Specimen storage conditions in Entebbe met standard conditions, including daily monitoring of temperature, and ensured lasting specimen quality. Laboratory testing was carried out both on site (for serological tests – Rapid HIV test, syphilis rapid test, CD4 count for the Kampala site) and off site (peripheral hub site and some at regional referral hospitals/hubs whereas others were shipped to CPHL and others to Atlanta).

context: A standardized data collection instrument was used to collect data for all survey groups. This instrument was designed in Questionnaire Design Studio (QDS 5.0) with validations, group specific and logical skips and AUDIT functions to measure and automatically score someone according to the risk associated with specific self-reported behavior. The ACASI was the main data collection instrument along with the computer-Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI), administered by survey staff if needed. Data was collected on characteristics like demographics, HIV-relevant behaviours, symptoms of STIs, as well as on HIV-related knowledge, attitude, practices, stigma, perceptions, and questions related to mental health or other health-related aspects. Each interview lasted between 45-90 minutes, depending on the participant's responsiveness and speed.
Determining Target sample size

For surveys with an HIV prevalence of >10%, the target sample size aimed to estimate VLS with a precision of no more than +/- 10 percentage points. Assuming a design effect of 2 in RDS surveys (Salganik et al., 2006, Salganik et al., 2010), this meant that to collect VL results for about 200 participants (see table below for varying scenarios). Our total target sample size therefore would vary between 500 and 1,700 (larger HIV prevalence may require smaller sample sizes). Further we monitored convergence and bottleneck graphs for VLS and HIV prevalence (See Annex 6) and would continue sampling (and introduce new seeds) if convergence had not been reached for both indicators or severe bottlenecks are observed
To accommodate still circulating (valid) RDS coupons after coupon issuance had been stopped, the final sample sizes slightly exceeded the needed sample sizes or the maximum sample size stated here.

2.4 Seeds and Enrolment

Seeds were participants who initiated in each referral chain. A seed was a participant who was purposely selected by the investigators in collaboration with the CBOs. Seed selection prioritized individuals with large social networks, positive community standing, and alignment with survey objectives. To ensure independence and diversity, seeds were chosen from various backgrounds based on age, place of residence, education, socioeconomic status. Seeds met the respective eligibility criteria and were given coupons and instructions for peer recruitment.

Seeds and subsequent participants received 3 coupons at the beginning of the survey and as time progressed, the number of coupons given to recruits per survey group varied, depending on the proportion of coupons redeemed, to facilitate continued waves, and to enable attainment of the desired sampling size. Due to the varying local contexts of these survey sites that is the social economic, cultural diversities of these environments, enrolment and participation in some areas required bigger or greater number of seeds to try and capture higher, diverse respondents or create new waves of participants to obtain the sample size and also sustain the survey. context: Data analysis was done using several statistical software i.e., STATA, R and RDS Analyst. We used Gile’s SS estimator in the RDS Analyst (RDSA) R package to generate weights and then obtained weighted estimates in R and or STATA. For the pooled analysis, we applied the proportional site-level PSE method. First, the absolute MAR population size estimates (PSE) across all locations were summed to obtain the total MAR PSE. Next, the site-specific PSE was divided by the total PSE to determine the proportional contribution of each site. Finally, the MAR survey weights for each site were adjusted by multiplying them with the corresponding site-specific proportional PSE.
2.6 Ethical Considerations

Prior to the beginning of the survey, Crane Survey held consultations with the populations at risk of HIV across all the survey sites. These were to be involved in the design, implementation, report writing and dissemination phases to ensure inclusivity and relevance. Protocol approval was obtained from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH) Higher Degrees Research and Ethics Committee (HDREC) Institutional Review Board (IRB), the Population Council IRB, and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST).

rows: This section highlights that avoidance of care reflects anticipated stigma rather than direct denial of services. This can be clearly observed in Kampala, where 67% participant responded avoiding health care due to stigma but only 18% have ever been denied care (anticipated stigma>than experienced stigma). rows: Overall self-reported HIV prevalence was 6.3%, with significant site variation from 1.8% in Fort Portal to 13.1% in Lira. Hospitals and clinics were the most frequent testing modality (47.0%), and while most participants reported respectful treatment from providers (91.2%), this varied by site.

3.5 Progress towards UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets
rows: Pooled results show 86.1% of people living with HIV (PLHIV) were aware of their status (the "first 95"). Among those aware, 99.8% reported being on ART (the "second 95"), and of those on treatment, 91.6% were virally suppressed (the "third 95"). However, these overall figures mask extreme variability and instability at the site level, driven by very small sample sizes. For instance, awareness of status (the "first 95") ranged from an estimated 38.3% in Gulu to 87.9% in Jinja. The subsequent targets for treatment and viral suppression are often based on denominators too small to yield meaningful estimates (e.g., n=2 in Fort Portal). The unconditional cascade, which measures the proportion of all PLHIV who are virally suppressed, was 78.7% overall but showed significant gaps in sites like Mbarara (29.0%) and Gulu (25.1%). Due to numerous inconsistencies in how denominators are defined and applied across the tables, these cascade estimates should be re-evaluated before being interpreted as program performance.

3.6 Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) use characteristics among HIV Negative MAR surveyed in 8 districts of Uganda, 2022-2023
rows: This section presents results on PrEP use among HIV-negative MAR. Overall, 66.0% of participants had heard of PrEP, though awareness varied substantially by site, from 33.2% in Arua to 82.3% in Fort Portal. Of those aware of PrEP, only 37.5% reported ever being offered it, while 60.6% knew where to access it. Across all HIV-negative participants, 55.2% expressed a desire to use PrEP. However, recent uptake was low, with 12.8% of those aware reporting use in the last 7 days and 12.1% in the last 6 months. Among those who had heard of PrEP, 64.4% had never used it. For participants not currently on PrEP, the most cited reasons for non-use included fear of side effects (22.0%), lack of knowledge about where to access it (18.8%), and concern that people may think they have HIV (16.6%).

rows: This section presents results for TB screening and treatment. Among people living with HIV (PLHIV), only 33.8% reported being screened for TB symptoms after their diagnosis, with a majority (61.3%) unable to recall. Among HIV-negative participants, 27.4% reported being screened. For the small subset of PLHIV who were screened (N=54), 24.6% reported being told they had TB. Among those screened and not diagnosed with active TB (N=41), 87.0% reported receiving TB Preventive Therapy (TPT), indicating high TPT coverage within this specific group. However, among the very few diagnosed with active TB (N=10), a significant data gap exists, with 88.8% not providing a response about receiving treatment, making the treatment estimate unreliable.

3.8 Alcohol use among MAR surveyed in 8 districts of Uganda, 2022-2023
rows: Overall, 54.3% of participants reported consuming alcohol within the last 12 months, while 32.0% reported never drinking. There was significant site-level variation in recent alcohol use, ranging from 42.8% in Masaka and 48.3% in Jinja to 69.3% in Fort Portal. Among those who drank in the last 12 months, consumption patterns varied: 33.5% drank 2-4 times a month, while 31.7% drank monthly or less. On a typical day of drinking, the most common quantity was one drink or less (48.0%). Based on a likely data inversion, reported alcohol abuse appears to be around 9.0% overall, a figure that still warrants attention.

3.9 Mental health characteristics among MAR surveyed in 8 districts of Uganda, 2021-2023
rows: Depressive symptoms were prevalent, with 15.5% of participants reporting little interest or pleasure in doing things nearly every day in the last two weeks, and 15.6% feeling down, depressed, or hopeless with the same frequency. The prevalence of these daily symptoms varied widely by site, from 8.6% in Arua to 42.4% in Lira. Based on a composite score, 33.5% of all participants had symptoms consistent with some or severe depression, and a "likely depression" screener was met by 9.6% of the sample. However, there are significant inconsistencies in how these measures are applied and reported at the site level. For example, Arua reported 0% "likely depression" despite a third of its participants showing some or severe symptoms. Self-reported diagnoses were less common than symptoms, with 5.5% of the total sample reporting a depression diagnosis and 10.5% reporting an anxiety diagnosis in the last six months.

3.13 Viral Load and CD4 Count Characteristics among MAR in 8 districts of Uganda, 2022-2023
rows: Viral Load and CD4 Count summary

The median CD4 count was 492.7, with 57.2% of participants having a CD4 count in Stage 1 (≥500 cells/mm³), indicating a generally strong immune status. For viral load, 57.5% of participants had a suppressed viral load of less than 50 copies/mL. However, 17.6% had a high viral load of over 999 copies/mL. Among a subset of participants, 62.4% were aware of the "Undetectable = Untransmittable" (U=U) concept. Significant portions of data regarding VL testing history were not provided, limiting a full assessment of monitoring coverage.
